To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the CO2 pressure in rebreathed gases was always higher than that in systemic arterial blood; (2) the difference increased with exercise intensity but was not affected by prolonged rebreathing; (3) the CO2 contents of arterial blood samples were always lower than that in rebreathed air; (4) these findings did not affect estimates of cardiac output based on indirect Fick methods.

the CO 2 pressure in arterial blood during prolonged rebreathing is less than that in the rebreathed gas, and that the difference between the two is not constant but increases with the level of exercise.

the CO 2 tensions of systemic arterial blood and pulmonary arterial blood, during rebreathing at rest or during exercise, are lower than those of the rebreathed gases, and that these differences are not constant, but increase with the level of effort.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the measurement of cardiac output and its distribution.
the estimation of the CO 2 pressure in systemic arterial blood from the tension in the rebreathed gas.
the measurement of cardiac output in man by indirect methods.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the rebreathing method of estimating cardiac output, as used in this study, is satisfactory for clinical purposes.
the indirect Fick and oxygen based estimates of CO are not in error, but the rebreathing estimates on which they are based do not represent the CO 2 tension of systemic arterial blood.
the CO 2 tensions in arterial blood are not significantly different from those in rebreathed air during exercise and that the indirect Fick estimates of cardiac output are reliable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the CO 2 tension and content of systemic arterial blood during exercise are not greatly different from those in mixed venous blood and that the indirect Fick and oxygen methods of estimating cardiac output are valid.

the CO 2 content of systemic arterial blood is lower than that of rebreathed gas during exercise, that the difference increases with the level of effort but is not affected by the time of sampling, and that the CO 4 content of pulmonary arterial blood is also lower than that of the rebreathed gas.
the CO 2 tensions in arterial blood during rebreathting are consistently lower than those in rebreathed gases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
rebreathing is not the ideal method for estimating mixed venous blood gases.
the CO 2 content of the arterial blood is a better measure of the arterial CO 2 tension than the CO 2 tension measured in arterial blood.
the indirect Fick technique for the estimation of cardiac output is not as robust as is often assumed.
